--- number-offset: 3 --- # Data Visualization with Seaborn and Matplotlib {#sec-ch04} A spreadsheet containing 600 rows of numbers conveys virtually nothing at a glance. A well-designed statistical visualization of that same data reveals in seconds where observations cluster, which values are anomalous, how experimental groups diverge, and how constructs covary. Graphics are not cosmetic embellishments appended to an empirical report at the conclusion; they are primary instruments of scientific discovery. The first task of an investigator encountering new data is to inspect it visually, and many data-entry anomalies and invalid assumptions are detected solely through graphical exploration. A figure is also a scientific argument. Visual design choices—the selected geometry, axis scaling, aspect ratio, color palette, and data aggregation—determine what a reader notices first and what conclusions they infer. Thoughtful choices clarify subtle empirical patterns; careless choices distort differences, exaggerating trivial variations or masking substantial heterogeneity. This chapter begins with graphical perception theory: what scientific figures are for, how human vision decodes visual encodings, and what constitutes an honest, truthful display. It then introduces **Seaborn** and **Matplotlib**, Python's standard libraries for statistical visualization, applying them to explore graduate student life (RQ1). ::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"} ## By the end of this chapter you will be able to - Explain why visualization is indispensable alongside summary statistics, and contrast exploratory vs. explanatory graphics. - Apply graphical perception theory, recognizing why position and length are decoded more accurately than angles, areas, or color saturation. - Select the appropriate visualization based on the research question and variable measurement levels. - Construct statistical graphics using Seaborn and Matplotlib (histograms, KDE density curves, bar charts, box plots, scatter plots, and line charts). - Build small multiples (facets) and correlation heatmaps to investigate multi-variable interactions. - Detect and rectify misleading visual representations (such as truncated bar-chart baselines and visual clutter). - Export publication-ready, high-resolution figures (300+ DPI PNG, PDF, SVG) formatted to journal dimensions. ::: ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"} **Teaching & Practice:** [Interactive Lecture Slides](../slides/04-data-visualization.html) · [Browser Playground Exercises](../playground/chapter04.html) ::: ## What a graph is for Summary statistics compress empirical distributions into a handful of numerical parameters (means, standard deviations, correlations). That compression can conceal radically different data distributions. The statistician Francis Anscombe demonstrated this vulnerability with four synthetic datasets constructed in 1973 [@anscombe1973], bundled in Seaborn as `anscombe`: ::: {.cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} anscombe = sns.load_dataset("anscombe") summary = ( anscombe .groupby("dataset") .agg( mean_x=("x", "mean"), sd_x=("x", "std"), mean_y=("y", "mean"), sd_y=("y", "std") ) .round(2) ) summary ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
mean_x sd_x mean_y sd_y
dataset
I 9.0 3.32 7.5 2.03
II 9.0 3.32 7.5 2.03
III 9.0 3.32 7.5 2.03
IV 9.0 3.32 7.5 2.03
``` ::: ::: Across all four datasets, the summary statistics are practically identical: $\bar{x} = 9.0$, $s_x = 3.32$, $\bar{y} = 7.50$, and $s_y = 2.03$. Bivariate regression yields identical linear fits ($y = 3.0 + 0.5x$) with identical correlation coefficients ($r = 0.82$). Judged solely by numerical summaries, the four datasets appear indistinguishable. Yet @fig-anscombe demonstrates that their underlying relationships are entirely dissimilar. ::: {.cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = sns.lmplot( data=anscombe, x="x", y="y", col="dataset", col_wrap=2, ci=None, height=2.5, aspect=1.3, scatter_kws={"s": 35, "color": "#1f77b4"}, line_kws={"color": "grey", "linewidth": 1.5} ) g.set_axis_labels("X", "Y") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Anscombe's quartet: identical means, standard deviations, and regression lines, but four completely different empirical patterns.](04-data-visualization_files/figure-typst/fig-anscombe-output-1.svg){#fig-anscombe fig-alt='Four scatter plots with identical linear regression slopes. Dataset I is a noisy linear relationship; Dataset II is a smooth parabolic curve; Dataset III is a perfect line with a single outlier; Dataset IV shows points stacked vertically with one extreme leverage point.'} ::: ::: Only Dataset I represents the bivariate linear association assumed by Pearson's $r$. Dataset II is a non-linear quadratic curve, Dataset III is a perfect linear relationship corrupted by one outlier, and Dataset IV is an unassociated vertical cluster whose correlation is produced entirely by a single high-leverage point. An analyst relying strictly on summary statistics would draw identical—and incorrect—conclusions across all four. Visual inspection prior to modeling is not optional; it is a prerequisite for valid inference. ### Exploratory versus explanatory graphs Scientific graphics serve two distinct functions: - **Exploratory graphs:** Created rapidly by the researcher to interrogate the data—checking skewness, detecting outliers, and screening for interaction effects. They require minimal aesthetic polish. - **Explanatory graphs:** Curated for external readers and thesis examiners to communicate a validated empirical finding. They require meticulous care: informative axis labels, accessible color palettes, annotations, and the elimination of extraneous chartjunk. ## Graphical perception: How vision decodes data Graphs function by translating numbers into visual encodings: position, length, angle, area, slope, and color. Human perception does not decode these attributes with equal precision. In pioneering experiments, William Cleveland and Robert McGill [@cleveland1984] evaluated how accurately observers judge quantitative differences across visual channels, establishing an empirical hierarchy: 1. **Position along a common aligned scale** (most accurate) 2. **Length** 3. **Slope and Angle** 4. **Area** 5. **Color saturation and hue** (least accurate) Effective scientific graphics map primary research comparisons to position or length, reserving color and area for secondary grouping. The perceptual difference is readily apparent when comparing identical proportions displayed as a pie chart versus a bar chart (@fig-pie-bar). ::: {.cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} shares = pd.DataFrame({ "group": ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"], "percent": [23, 21, 20, 19, 17] }) fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.5, 3.2)) # Pie chart (angle / area) ax1.pie(shares["percent"], labels=shares["group"], startangle=90, colors=sns.color_palette("mako", 5)) ax1.set_title("Pie chart (Angle / Area)", fontsize=11) # Bar chart (aligned length) sns.barplot(data=shares, x="group", y="percent", color="#4c72b0", ax=ax2) ax2.set(title="Bar chart (Aligned Length)", xlabel="Category", ylabel="Percentage (%)") ax2.set_ylim(0, 26) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The same five percentages displayed as a pie chart (angle and area) versus a bar chart (length along an aligned scale). Identifying the ranking is immediate in the bar chart.](04-data-visualization_files/figure-typst/fig-pie-bar-output-1.svg){#fig-pie-bar fig-alt='Side-by-side comparison. Left: a pie chart with five nearly identical slices labelled A through E. Right: an aligned bar chart where the steady decline from A to E is obvious.'} ::: ::: In the pie chart, the five slices appear virtually identical; determining the rank order requires scrutinizing legends and mentally comparing angles. In the bar chart, the monotonic decline from category A (23%) to E (17%) is evident immediately because comparisons occur along a common baseline. Consequently, scientific reporting favors bar charts and dot plots over pie charts. ## Selecting the right visualization The choice of graph is governed by the research question and the levels of measurement of the variables under study (@tbl-which-graph). | Analytical Question | Variable Types | Recommended Graph | Python Seaborn / Matplotlib Function | |---|---|---|---| | Distribution of a single continuous metric | One numeric | Histogram / KDE plot | `sns.histplot()`, `sns.kdeplot()` | | Frequency counts of categorical groups | One categorical | Bar chart | `sns.countplot()`, `sns.barplot()` | | Comparison of continuous metric across groups | One numeric by categorical | Box plot / Strip plot | `sns.boxplot()`, `sns.stripplot()` | | Association between two continuous variables | Two numeric | Scatter plot with trend line | `sns.scatterplot()`, `sns.regplot()` | | Trajectory of a metric over time | Numeric over time | Longitudinal line plot | `sns.lineplot()` | | Multilateral correlation structure | Several numeric | Correlation heatmap | `sns.heatmap()` | : Selecting the appropriate visualization based on analytical questions and variable types {#tbl-which-graph} ## Core statistical visualizations with Seaborn To explore Elaf's wellbeing cohort, we merge Semester 1 measurements with baseline student background demographics: ::: {.cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} first_sem = ( semesters .query("semester == 1") .merge(students, on="student_id", how="left") ) ``` ::: ### Histograms and density curves The initial question concerning any continuous variable addresses its empirical distribution: central tendency, spread, skewness, and the presence of extreme outliers. A **histogram** partitions the continuous range into discrete bins, displaying the count of observations falling within each interval: ::: {.cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5)) sns.histplot( data=first_sem, x="sleep_hours", binwidth=0.5, color="#4c72b0", edgecolor="white", ax=ax ) ax.set(xlabel="Hours of sleep per night", ylabel="Number of students") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Distribution of sleep hours per night in Semester 1.](04-data-visualization_files/figure-typst/fig-sleep-hist-output-1.svg){#fig-sleep-hist fig-alt='Histogram of sleep hours, roughly bell-shaped and centered near 6.5 hours, ranging between 3.5 and 10 hours.'} ::: ::: @fig-sleep-hist displays a roughly symmetrical, unimodal distribution centered near 6.5 hours. Exactly `r round(100 * share_short, 1)`% of graduate students sleep less than the clinically recommended 7 hours during their first semester. ### Bar charts for categorical counts A **bar chart** plots frequency distributions across categorical factor levels: ::: {.cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5)) sns.countplot( data=students, x="faculty", color="#4c72b0", order=students["faculty"].value_counts().index, ax=ax ) ax.set(xlabel="Faculty", ylabel="Student Count") plt.xticks(rotation=20, ha="right") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Enrollment frequency across academic faculties.](04-data-visualization_files/figure-typst/fig-faculty-bar-output-1.svg){#fig-faculty-bar fig-alt='Bar chart displaying the number of students per faculty: Health Sciences and Education have the highest counts.'} ::: ::: Because bar lengths represent quantities proportionally, the numerical baseline must always start at zero. ### Box plots for group comparisons A **box plot** summarizes five key distribution parameters: the median (center line), interquartile range (IQR, box edges covering the 25th to 75th percentiles), whiskers (extending to $1.5 \times \text{IQR}$), and individual points for potential outliers. It is the gold standard for comparing continuous metrics across qualitative groups: ::: {.cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 3.5)) sns.boxplot( data=first_sem, x="study_mode", y="wellbeing", palette=["#4c72b0", "#55a868"], ax=ax, width=0.5 ) ax.set(xlabel="Study Mode", ylabel="Wellbeing Index (0 to 100)") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` C:\Users\polla\AppData\Local\Temp\ipykernel_54144\230693867.py:3: FutureWarning: Passing `palette` without assigning `hue` is deprecated and will be removed in v0.14.0. Assign the `x` variable to `hue` and set `legend=False` for the same effect. sns.boxplot( ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Wellbeing in Semester 1 by study mode (Full-time vs. Part-time).](04-data-visualization_files/figure-typst/fig-wellbeing-box-output-2.svg){#fig-wellbeing-box fig-alt='Two box plots showing that part-time students report slightly lower median wellbeing than full-time students, with substantial overlap.'} ::: ::: Part-time students report a slightly lower median wellbeing score than full-time students, but the distributions overlap substantially. In @sec-ch08, we use inferential ANOVA to test whether this group discrepancy is statistically significant. ### Scatter plots with regression trend lines The relationship between two continuous variables—such as sleep hours and academic performance—is evaluated via a **scatter plot**. When plotting 600 participants, individual markers often overlap (**overplotting**). We mitigate this by setting transparency (`alpha=0.4`) and overlaying a linear regression trend line with `sns.regplot()`: ::: {.cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.8)) sns.regplot( data=first_sem, x="sleep_hours", y="gpa", scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.35, "color": "#4c72b0"}, line_kws={"color": "#c44e52", "linewidth": 2}, ax=ax ) ax.set(xlabel="Hours of sleep per night", ylabel="Grade Point Average (GPA)") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Association between sleep hours and GPA in Semester 1, with ordinary least squares trend line.](04-data-visualization_files/figure-typst/fig-sleep-gpa-output-1.svg){#fig-sleep-gpa fig-alt='Scatter plot of GPA against sleep hours showing a positive linear slope: students who sleep longer tend to achieve slightly higher GPAs, with substantial scatter.'} ::: ::: The regression line slopes upward: students sleeping more hours tend to achieve modestly higher GPAs. However, observations scatter broadly around the line ($r \approx 0.30$), indicating that sleep explains only a fraction of total academic variance. ### Longitudinal trajectory line plots Elaf's research design tracked cohorts across four consecutive semesters. A **line plot** illustrates how group means evolve over time: ::: {.cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} wellbeing_trajectory = ( semesters .merge(students[["student_id", "workshop"]], on="student_id", how="left") .groupby(["semester", "workshop"])["wellbeing"] .mean() .reset_index() ) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.8)) sns.lineplot( data=wellbeing_trajectory, x="semester", y="wellbeing", hue="workshop", marker="o", markersize=7, linewidth=2, palette={"Invited": "#2ca02c", "Not invited": "#7f7f7f"}, ax=ax ) ax.set( title="Cohort Wellbeing Trajectory Over Two Years", xlabel="Academic Semester", ylabel="Mean Wellbeing (0 to 100)", xticks=[1, 2, 3, 4] ) ax.legend(title="Workshop Group", frameon=True) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Longitudinal wellbeing trajectories across four semesters by workshop participation.](04-data-visualization_files/figure-typst/fig-wellbeing-lines-output-1.svg){#fig-wellbeing-lines fig-alt='Two trajectory lines spanning Semesters 1 to 4. Baseline scores in Semester 1 are identical; from Semester 2 onward, invited workshop participants achieve approximately 5 points higher wellbeing.'} ::: ::: @fig-wellbeing-lines captures the core narrative of Elaf's intervention study: groups start at identical baselines in Semester 1, invited students pull ahead following the intervention in Semester 2, and the gap stabilizes over subsequent terms. ## Preparing publication-quality figures Exploratory graphics suffice during initial data exploration, but explanatory figures destined for a thesis or journal article require publication-standard polish. ### Annotations and reference lines Adding explicit reference lines and annotations directs reader attention to clinically meaningful thresholds: ::: {.cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.8)) sns.histplot( data=first_sem, x="sleep_hours", binwidth=0.5, color="#4c72b0", edgecolor="white", ax=ax ) ax.axvline(7.0, color="#c44e52", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.8) ax.text( 7.1, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.9, "Recommended: 7.0 hrs", color="#c44e52", fontweight="semibold", verticalalignment="top" ) ax.set( title="Baseline Sleep Duration", xlabel="Hours of sleep per night", ylabel="Number of students" ) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` findfont: Failed to find font weight semibold for Arial, now using 700. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Distribution of sleep hours with clinical 7-hour reference benchmark.](04-data-visualization_files/figure-typst/fig-annotated-output-2.svg){#fig-annotated fig-alt='Histogram of sleep hours with a vertical dashed line positioned at 7 hours, annotated with \'Recommended benchmark: 7 hours\'.'} ::: ::: ### Color accessibility Approximately 8% of men and 0.5% of women experience congenital color vision deficiency (red-green color blindness). A scientific graphic must remain interpretable to all readers and reproduce legibly when printed in black and white: - Avoid rainbow (`jet`) palettes, which introduce artificial visual boundaries. - Utilize perceptually uniform, colorblind-safe palettes such as `viridis`, `plasma`, `cividis`, or `colorblind`. - Combine color with redundant visual encodings (distinct marker shapes, line styles, or direct text labels). ## Honest graphs and visual ethics A visualization can be mathematically accurate while remaining visually misleading. Distortion frequently stems from unexamined software defaults: 1. **Truncated vertical baselines on bar charts:** Because a bar encodes magnitude through length, truncating the baseline exaggerates differences. 2. **Extreme aspect ratios:** Altering aspect ratios artificially steepens or flattens longitudinal trends. 3. **Chartjunk and 3D effects:** Pseudo-3D perspectives distort angular perception and distance. 4. **Hiding underlying distribution variance:** Reporting only summary bar heights masks critical within-group heterogeneity. ### Redesigning a misleading figure Suppose an investigator evaluates whether mean wellbeing differs across faculties. A careless chart with an artificially truncated axis appears in @fig-before: ::: {.cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} faculty_means = ( first_sem .groupby("faculty")["wellbeing"] .mean() .reset_index() ) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.5)) sns.barplot(data=faculty_means, x="faculty", y="wellbeing", palette="Blues_d", ax=ax) ax.set_ylim(58, 62.5) # Truncated baseline! ax.set(title="Misleading: Truncated Baseline (58 to 62.5)", xlabel="Faculty", ylabel="Mean Wellbeing") plt.xticks(rotation=20, ha="right") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` C:\Users\polla\AppData\Local\Temp\ipykernel_54144\2329551519.py:9: FutureWarning: Passing `palette` without assigning `hue` is deprecated and will be removed in v0.14.0. Assign the `x` variable to `hue` and set `legend=False` for the same effect. sns.barplot(data=faculty_means, x="faculty", y="wellbeing", palette="Blues_d", ax=ax) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![A misleading graphic: the vertical axis is truncated at 58, exaggerating modest differences and concealing student-level variance.](04-data-visualization_files/figure-typst/fig-before-output-2.svg){#fig-before fig-alt='Bar chart of average wellbeing across five faculties with the vertical axis starting at 58. Education appears several times higher than Social Sciences.'} ::: ::: In @fig-before, the Education faculty bar appears triple the height of Social Sciences. Yet the actual group means differ by barely 2.5 points on a 100-point scale. Furthermore, the bar chart completely conceals individual variation. In @fig-after, the display is redesigned into an honest, informative jittered strip plot with overlaid group means: ::: {.cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} order = faculty_means.sort_values("wellbeing")["faculty"] fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8)) # Jittered individual student scores sns.stripplot( data=first_sem, y="faculty", x="wellbeing", order=order, color="grey", alpha=0.3, jitter=0.2, size=5, ax=ax ) # Overlay group means as prominent diamonds sns.pointplot( data=first_sem, y="faculty", x="wellbeing", order=order, color="#c44e52", markers="D", scale=0.8, errorbar=None, join=False, ax=ax ) ax.set( title="Truthful: Student Wellbeing Distribution by Faculty", xlabel="Wellbeing Index (0 to 100)", ylabel=None, xlim=(0, 100) # Full theoretical scale! ) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` C:\Users\polla\AppData\Local\Temp\ipykernel_54144\1426493859.py:12: UserWarning: The `scale` parameter is deprecated and will be removed in v0.15.0. scores vary widely between 25 and 95 across all departments, and average differences between faculties are trivial by comparison. ## Advanced scientific visualizations ### Small multiples (Faceting) Small multiples partition a complex visualization into separate subpanels sharing identical axes, enabling direct visual comparisons: ::: {.cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = sns.lmplot( data=first_sem, x="sleep_hours", y="gpa", col="programme", scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.35, "color": "#4c72b0"}, line_kws={"color": "#c44e52"}, height=3.5, aspect=1.1 ) g.set_axis_labels("Hours of Sleep per Night", "GPA") g.set_titles(col_template="{col_name} Candidates") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Association between sleep hours and GPA, faceted by degree programme.](04-data-visualization_files/figure-typst/fig-facets-output-1.svg){#fig-facets fig-alt='Two scatter plots side by side for Master\'s and PhD students, each displaying an identical positive slope between sleep and GPA.'} ::: ::: The regression slope between sleep and academic performance is virtually identical across both Master's and PhD cohorts. ### Kernel density estimation (KDE) plots A **density plot** provides a smoothed continuous estimate of the probability density function, facilitating clean comparisons of overlapping distributions: ::: {.cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} sem2_data = ( semesters .query("semester == 2") .merge(students[["student_id", "workshop"]], on="student_id") ) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.5)) sns.kdeplot( data=sem2_data, x="wellbeing", hue="workshop", fill=True, common_norm=False, alpha=0.35, palette={"Invited": "#2ca02c", "Not invited": "#7f7f7f"}, linewidth=2, ax=ax ) ax.set( title="Semester 2 Post-Intervention Wellbeing Distribution", xlabel="Wellbeing Index (0 to 100)", ylabel="Probability Density" ) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Comparative probability density of Semester 2 wellbeing by workshop group.](04-data-visualization_files/figure-typst/fig-density-output-1.svg){#fig-density fig-alt='Two overlapping smooth density curves. The curve for invited workshop participants is visibly shifted to the right of the uninvited group.'} ::: ::: Notice that the entire distribution for invited students is shifted rightward, demonstrating a cohort-wide positive effect rather than an isolated outlier reaction. ### Correlation heatmaps When examining relationships among numerous continuous constructs, a **correlation heatmap** visualizes the bivariate correlation matrix via a diverging color gradient: ::: {.cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} corr_vars = first_sem[["gpa", "sleep_hours", "study_hours", "wellbeing"]].corr() fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4.2)) sns.heatmap( corr_vars, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap="vlag", vmin=-1.0, vmax=1.0, center=0.0, square=True, linewidths=0.5, cbar_kws={"shrink": 0.8}, ax=ax ) ax.set_title("Correlation Heatmap (Semester 1)", fontsize=11, pad=10) plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Bivariate correlation matrix across Semester 1 quantitative metrics.](04-data-visualization_files/figure-typst/fig-heatmap-output-1.svg){#fig-heatmap fig-alt='A 4-by-4 correlation matrix of colored cells displaying correlation coefficients between GPA, sleep hours, study hours, and wellbeing.'} ::: ::: The diverging `vlag` palette centers white at zero correlation, mapping negative associations to blue and positive associations to red. Values printed within each cell ensure readers are not forced to decode coefficients solely through color saturation. ## Exporting publication-ready figures Scientific figures must be exported at explicit target physical dimensions and print resolutions: ```python # Save as 300 DPI PNG raster image (suitable for Word documents and presentations): fig.savefig("figures/wellbeing_trajectory.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight") # Save as vector graphic (ideal for LaTeX and journal publication): fig.savefig("figures/wellbeing_trajectory.pdf", bbox_inches="tight") ``` Setting `bbox_inches="tight"` prevents axis labels from being clipped. Standard journal column widths typically measure 8.5 cm (single column) or 17.5 cm (full width). Defining figure sizes in code preserves font proportions when rendered on the printed page. ## Chapter review ### Summary - Summary statistics can mask fundamentally divergent distributions (Anscombe's quartet); visualizing data prior to modeling is essential. - Graphical perception theory demonstrates that position and length are decoded with greatest precision; key scientific comparisons must be mapped to aligned coordinates. - Continuous distributions are inspected using histograms and KDE density plots; group comparisons rely on box plots and strip plots; bivariate relationships are evaluated via scatter plots and regression trend lines. - Tidy longitudinal trajectories are plotted using `sns.lineplot()`, small multiples using `sns.lmplot(col=...)`, and correlation matrices using `sns.heatmap()`. - Ethical visual design requires zero-aligned baselines for bar charts, colorblind-accessible palettes (`viridis`, `vlag`), and transparent representation of within-group variance. - Publication-quality figures are saved using `fig.savefig()` at 300+ DPI or vector formats (`.pdf`, `.svg`). ### Key terms Anscombe's quartet, exploratory vs. explanatory graphics, graphical perception, aligned scale, histogram, KDE density plot, box plot, strip plot, overplotting, regression trend line, longitudinal line plot, small multiples, facet, correlation heatmap, color accessibility, chartjunk, DPI, vector graphics. ## Exercises Work through these exercises in your browser using the [Chapter 4 Playground](../playground/chapter04.html) or download the starter project for VS Code. 1. Using `first_sem`, generate a histogram of `study_hours`. Experiment with binwidths of 2, 5, and 10 hours, and evaluate which binning best reveals distribution shape. 2. Construct a bar chart showing student counts across `employment` categories, ordered from `"None"` to `"Full-time job"`, using a colorblind-safe single color. 3. Generate box plots comparing Semester 1 GPA across academic faculties, formatting axis labels clearly. 4. Draw a scatter plot of caffeine consumption (`caffeine_mg`) against sleep hours (`sleep_hours`) in Semester 1 with an overlaid linear regression line, and describe the observed association. 5. Save any figure created in this chapter to `figures/exercise_plot.png` at 300 DPI with tight bounding boxes. 6. Redesign the faculty wellbeing bar chart into a horizontal strip plot showing both individual scores and group medians. Explain why this display is scientifically superior. ## Further reading - *Fundamentals of Data Visualization* by Claus O. Wilke [@wilke2019]: an exceptional, language-agnostic text on the principles of honest, effective visual communication. - Official documentation for [Seaborn](https://seaborn.pydata.org/) and [Matplotlib](https://matplotlib.org/). - "Graphical Perception" by William S.
